text:
B: Hi. Erm, can you hear me?
A: Yes. Hello.
B: Hi, I'm Abena. I'm in Chelmsford.
A: Agnieszka. Wakefield. You are a student, yes? I can see the hoodie.
B: Yeah, first year, biomedical science. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous. You kind of remind me of my teachers at sixth form.
A: I am a teacher. Maths. So you are right. But I am not marking you, so you can relax.
B: [laughs] Okay. That helps, actually.
A: Biomedical. Do you have statistics?
B: Yeah, there's a module this term. I'm okay with it, I think. I just like to check everything like three times.
A: Good. Check three times. Most of my students check zero times and then they are surprised.
B: I think I'd be one of your quiet ones. I sit at the front and I only answer if I'm sure.
A: The quiet ones at the front are the ones who pass. The loud ones at the back, I spend my life with them. Year 8. Feral.
B: [laughs] My brother's fourteen, so I kind of know what you mean. He uses all the hot water and then sings in the shower.
A: My son is seventeen. He doesn't sing, he just eats. Everything. I buy food Monday, Wednesday it is gone.
B: That's exactly my brother. Erm, sorry, are you from Wakefield originally?
A: No, Poland. Tarnów, south of Poland. I came 2006, I was thirty-two.
B: Oh, okay. I was born in Ghana, in Kumasi. We moved here when I was six, for my dad's nursing job.
A: Six. So you are more English than me, probably.
B: Kind of? I don't know. Erm, I understand Twi, but I answer my mum in English, and she teases me about it all the time.
A: My son does the same! I speak Polish, he answers English. Every time. I ask in Polish "did you eat my cheese," and he says "no" in English.
B: [laughs] That's so similar.
A: It's normal. The children are from here. We are from, I don't know. Somewhere in the middle.
B: Yeah. That's kind of how it feels. Like I'm not fully either. Sorry, that's quite a serious thing to say in three minutes.
A: No, it's true. It doesn't go away. You just get used to it. I say "tea" now for the evening meal. My sister in Poland thinks I am lost.
B: We say dinner. My mum makes jollof on Saturdays, and honestly, hers is better than anyone's.
A: Everyone's mother cooks the best. This is a law. What do you do when you don't study?
B: I read a lot. And I do botanical drawings, those on the wall.
A: I read crime novels. Polish, Scandinavian. Somebody dies on page one, by the end the detective knows who. Simple.
B: I've never really read crime. What would you recommend for someone who's—
A: Start with—
